Rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) attain a maximum recorded total length of 120 cm [Li = 120 cm], placing them among the larger-bodied salmonids native to Pacific drainages of North America. This ultimate length, typically observed in anadromous steelhead morphs, contrasts markedly with the size at which reproductive maturation occurs. Field surveys indicate that females begin their first spawning event at a forked length of 54 cm [Lp = 54 cm], a threshold that reflects a trade-off between somatic growth and the onset of gonadal recrudescence. At this stage, the wet weight at puberty has been measured at 3500 grams [Wwp = 3500 grams], representing a substantial fraction of the ultimate wet weight of 25400 grams [Wwi = 25400 grams] that large adults can achieve when conditions favor prolonged growth in productive riverine or lacustrine habitats.

Embryonic development in this species is highly dependent on thermal conditions, with laboratory incubation experiments revealing pronounced variation in hatching and emergence timing. At a constant water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the age at hatching is 32 days , and the fully emerged alevin reaches what is termed age at birth at 54 days [ab = 54 days]. Colder conditions substantially extend these intervals; when eggs are incubated at 5 °C [T = 5 °C], the age at hatching increases to 67 days , and the age at birth lengthens to 119 days [ab = 119 days]. The weight at hatch for the large-egg strain used in this study is 0.0388 grams , while the weight at birth is 0.0321 grams , values derived from wet weight multiplied by the proportion of dry matter reported in Table 2.

The reproductive output of rainbow trout is characterized by a high fecundity typical of iteroparous salmonids. Females produce between 2000 and 3000 eggs per kilogram of body weight at approximately 2.5 reproductive events per year when water temperatures are near 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. The dry egg weight was determined from large eggs sampled during the peak spawning period; after correcting for moisture content, each egg had a dry mass of 0.0414 grams . This investment per offspring, though modest in absolute terms, represents a considerable cumulative energetic outlay given the thousands of eggs produced per spawning season in females exceeding 3500 grams body mass.

Life-history timing at colder temperatures reveals a remarkably protracted developmental schedule. At 5 °C [T = 5 °C], the maximum lifespan of rainbow trout is approximately 4015 days [am = approximately 4015 days], or just over 11 years, a longevity that allows multiple spawning opportunities across several seasons. This cold-water lifespan is consistent with the general pattern among salmonids, where lower thermal regimes slow metabolic and developmental rates considerably. The substantial variation in developmental pace across temperatures underscores the species' plasticity: the same life-history event can span drastically different durations depending on local thermal conditions. Such protracted development under cold conditions likely reflects an adaptive strategy to synchronize emergence with optimal spring resource availability, allowing juveniles to exploit the seasonal pulse of aquatic insect production.

First reproduction in rainbow trout occurs after an extended juvenile period when water temperatures are elevated. At 13 °C [T = 13 °C], the age at first reproduction is 628 days after hatching [tR = 628 days after hatching], a duration encompassing an initial embryonic phase of approximately 28 days followed by a rapid egg growth period commencing 20 months post-hatch, based on gonadosomatic index (GSI) assessments. This relatively fast track to maturity under warmer conditions contrasts with the much slower pace observed at 5 °C, where individuals may not reach first reproduction until well into their second year. The maximum recorded adult body mass of 25400 grams [Wwi = 25400 grams] is typically achieved only in the most productive environments, highlighting the plasticity inherent in the species' life-history repertoire. Such intraspecific variation underscores the importance of local thermal and trophic conditions in shaping population dynamics across the species' wide geographic range.
